articles.title: Reading the Bench: Predictions for Five October Federal Circuit Arguments
articles.content:
by Dennis Crouch

I've been tracking Federal Circuit oral arguments on my SCOTUSGate page.  This post looks at five arguments from the October session. One of these has already been decided: a week after argument, the court affirmed In re Burandt in a R.36 judgment without opinion.

I have also been training an AI model on predicting appeal outcomes based upon the  oral argument transcripts, and get into some predictions on each of the five:

  • Samsung Display v. ITC (domestic industry; Samsung about 70% to win a remand),
  • Taylor Made v. Costco (which court hears an arbitration appeal; the hardest call),
  • In re Burandt (the USPTO's old Sensitive Application Warning System),
  • CEMCO v. KPSI (assignor estoppel after Minerva; likely affirmed by a divided panel), and
  • Wuhan China Star v. Samsung Display (APA arguments in PTAB appeals; the clearest affirmance besides Burandt that is already decided).

articles.title: A Toothbrush, a Lost Patent, and 170 Years of Claim Drafting
articles.content:
by Dennis Crouch
I started pulling at a loose bristle this week and ended up doing a deep dive into the history of the American toothbrush. I came across a Library of Congress explanation that H.N. Wadsworth of Washington, D.C. received the first American Toothbrush patent in 1857. That sounded way too late to me. And, in fact, the Patent Office's records tell a different story.
In 1874 the Office published a three-volume Subject-Matter Index of Patents for Inventions covering every patent from 1790 through 1873. Page 163 has fourteen entries under the heading “Brush, Tooth.” Thirteen of them carry patent numbers, and Wadsworth's No. 18,653 is the lowest. But, the last one doesn't have any number assigned at all.
The number is missing because U.S. patents were not numbered until 1836, and most of the earlier records burned in the Patent Office fire that December. A Connecticut state table of early patents calls the same grant a “tooth brush for machinery” and marks the record as likely missing. That made me wonder whether this was a brush for people at all. So, I did more digging into this.I want to pause here to plug a new book that was just published: Unfettered Invention. For readers interested in the earliest American patents, Scott Guthery, Julie Burke, and Prof. Michael Risch have just published Unfettered Invention: How the X Patents Sparked Early American Technology (Docent Press 2026). The "X patents" are the patents issued from 1790 to 1836 -- like the Philos Blake patent discussed below. The Patent Office fire of December 1836 destroyed the originals, and the ones that were later restored were retroactively given numbers with an X prefix. For the book, the authors recovered hundreds of lost records and used them to tell stories of early American invention and of the first Patent Office.
The 1830 patent itself is lost. But, it turns out that the Journal of the Franklin Institute published a monthly list of new American patents, with the editor's remarks on each. The June 1830 issue has this one as No. 10 for March: “For a Folding, Pocket Tooth Brush; Philos Blake, New Haven, Connecticut, March 8.” Blake was a nephew of Eli Whitney and later a New Haven hardware maker., but the journal quotes his claim:
I do not claim to have originated the idea of making a tooth brush portable by enclosing it in a case, nor that of making the case serve the purpose of a handle when it is used, but I do claim the invention of connecting the brush to its case by a pivot, or revolving joint.
Philos Blake, patent of March 8, 1830, as quoted in 5 J. Franklin Inst. (n.s.) 364 (June 1830).
So, Wadsworth holds the earliest surviving American toothbrush patent, but Philos Blake beat him by 27 years. (A second small correction: the Library of Congress dates the Wadsworth patent November 7, 1857. The patent itself says November 17.)Once I found this patent claim, it pushed me to shift the post into one focusing on claim drafting strategy - using the toothbrush as the subject matter example.
Blake's 1830 patent starts by disclaiming what was already known (the brush in a case, and the case that doubles as a handle) and only then claims his improvement, the pivot. That is the logic of a Jepson claim, almost ninety years before Ex parte Jepson. The journal's editor was not impressed with the business case: “We should be very apprehensive that tooth brushes made as described by the patentee, must be sold at a price which would prevent their employment to any considerable extent.”
Next step in this expanding project was to pull every toothbrush patent I could find. That turned out to be about 7,000 patents since 1976 alone, plus a selection going back to Wadsworth and Blake. The rest of this post walks through how the claims have changed, what patent attorneys are doing today, and why.

articles.title: Subject Matter Eligibility Declarations: An Empirical Study of Rule 132 Evidence and Examiner Response
articles.content:
by Dennis Crouch
In December 2025, Director Squires invited applicants to begin filing special Rule 132 declarations focused on patent eligibility. He called these Subject Matter Eligibility Declarations, or SMEDs. The practice is slowly becoming more popular. My most recent search of USPTO dockets found 460, filed in 414 applications, and enough of them have had time to get examiner responses to get a sense of their effectiveness. About one third are successful by my count: the next examiner action either allows the case or drops the §101 rejection.
Finding them in the USPTO dockets has been a bit tricky. Until very recently, most eligibility declarations have been filed as plain Rule 132 declarations, mixed in with thousands of unexpected-results, enablement and inventor-disclosure declarations. And, because they are offering factual declarations, a substantial number (around 15%) never use legalese such as "eligibility" or "101." The Office has a new AF/D.SMED document filing code that should help see them more directly. Ultimately, I downloaded every Rule 130, 131 and 132 affidavit filed in a published application since December 4, 2025, ran each of the 6k through OCR, and parsed the text of each one to sort out the eligibility declarations: those offered to show that the claims are patent-eligible. Nearly all of the ones I found were filed in response to a §101 eligibility rejection; only a handful were filed proactively, before any such rejection.
The result: of the ~6,100 declarations filed in the period, 460 are eligibility declarations. The big news though - once an eligibility declaration is filed, the examiner usually keeps the rejection. In cases where the next action is on the record, about 25% of applications received a notice of allowance, another 9% received an office action that dropped §101, but about 66% got the same rejection again. I also looked at what else was in the response and what the examiner said about it. Nearly all of these applicants amended their claims along with the declaration, and amending did not separate the winners from the losers. When the rejection did go away, the examiner credited the declaration about half the time.

articles.title: Inter Partes Review (IPR) Filings Collapse to a New Normal
articles.content:
by Dennis Crouch

The fiscal year that ended September 30, 2026 closed with about 450 IPR petitions, a third of the 1,400 filed in FY2025 and even fewer than the 510 filed in FY2013, the program's first full year.

Petitions ran about 110 a month through mid-2025. They fell to 61 in November 2025 and 30 in December, and have stayed between 15 and 46 a month ever since. September 2026 came in at 37. There is no sign of a rebound, and also no sign of a further slide: the series has been flat at roughly 30 a month for nine months.

articles.title: PTAB Law School Moot Court Competition Set for Spring 2027
articles.content:
by Dennis Crouch

I’m hoping Mizzou will be able to field a team in the newly announced PTAB moot court competition in Spring 2027, offered in collaboration with Indiana University Maurer School of Law. Each team will submit one written brief and argue at least once before a panel of Administrative Patent Judges, and the finalists will be invited to argue in person at USPTO headquarters in Alexandria. There is no entry fee, but only a limited number of teams will be admitted. Interested schools should contact PTABMOOT@iu.edu. The PTAB previously ran a moot court in 2024-25 and this one looks to be a continuation of that with a bit more structure.

Law students (and anyone making <$75 per year) – get a free Patently-O subscription here.

The headline pitches the competition to “the PTAB advocates of tomorrow,” but it arrives with AIA trial work at a low point. Petitioners filed about 450 IPR petitions in FY2026, down from about 1,400 the year before — because would-be petitioners predict their case would be swiftly denied by Director Squires.  I do expect the numbers to rise again, but not until a new administration is in place, and we may continue to see yo-yoing over the next few years.
